title: Present perfect continuous and present perfect
subtitle: I've been playing / I've played
summary: Separate the process from the result, and know which verbs refuse the present perfect continuous.

lesson.heading: An activity in progress until recently
lesson.text: The present perfect continuous expresses an activity - a task, a piece of work - that was in progress until recently or until the moment of speaking. We often add a time expression saying how long it went on.

examples.text: **Have you been working** in the garden all day? You look exhausted.
She**'s been writing** the book since she was in her twenties and at last it's finished.

lesson.heading: Not with unchanging states
lesson.text: We don't use the present perfect continuous with verbs such as **belong, know, (dis)like** and **understand**, which describe unchanging states.

examples.text: **I haven't liked** ice cream since I ate too much and was sick.
**We've been looking** forward to this holiday for ages.
examples.note: or We've looked forward to ... - for general circumstances up to now, either form works

lesson.heading: Something that has just finished

left.label: Present perfect - one complete happening
examples: He**'s broken** his finger and is in a lot of pain. (not ~~He's been breaking~~)

right.label: Present perfect continuous - extended or repeated activity
examples: I**'ve been playing** squash and need a shower! (more likely than I've played ...)

lesson.note: Both are used for something recently finished whose results we can still see; the choice depends on the verb.

lesson.heading: Drawing a conclusion from the evidence
lesson.text: When we draw a conclusion from what we can see or hear, we prefer the present perfect continuous. It is a favourite form for complaining and criticising.

examples.text: Who**'s been messing** around with my papers? They're all over the place.
You**'ve been eating** chocolate, haven't you? There's some on your shirt.

left.label: The result - present perfect
examples: Prices **have decreased** by 7%. (not ~~Prices have been decreasing by 7%~~)
I**'ve used** three tins of paint on the kitchen walls. (not ~~I've been using three tins~~)

right.label: The process - either form
examples: Prices **have been decreasing** recently. (or Prices have decreased ...)
I**'ve been using** a new kind of paint on the kitchen walls. (or I've used ...)

lesson.heading: Ongoing and repeated, or a set number of times?
lesson.text: The present perfect continuous emphasises that an activity is ongoing and repeated. The present perfect suggests it happened once, or a specified number of times.

examples.text: Miguel **has been kicking** a football against the wall all day.
He **has played** for the national team in 65 matches so far.
examples.wrong: He has been playing for the national team in 65 matches so far

examples.text: The workers **have been calling** for the chairman's resignation.
examples.note: = a number of times, probably over an extended period

examples.text: Workers **have called** for management to begin negotiations on pay.
examples.note: = maybe a number of times, maybe only once

lesson.text: If the sentence contains a number - 7%, three tins, 65 matches - you are talking about a result, so use the plain present perfect.

exercises.prompt: We ___ at this hotel a couple of times before.
exercises.explanation: A specified number of occasions, so the plain present perfect.
This is a fact about your experience up to now, not an activity in progress.

exercises.prompt: He ___ his finger and is in a lot of pain.
exercises.explanation: Breaking a finger is one complete happening, so the present perfect continuous is impossible.

exercises.statement: Who's been messing around with my papers? They're all over the place.
exercises.explanation: Correct. We use the present perfect continuous to draw a conclusion from what we can see - often to complain.

exercises.prompt: I ___ this book on astrophysics for hours and I'm still only on page six.
exercises.explanation: An activity in progress with a time expression saying how long: the present perfect continuous is the natural choice.

exercises.prompt: Match the two halves of these sentences.

pairs.left: Have you been working in the garden all day?
You've been eating chocolate, haven't you?

pairs.right: since I ate too much and was sick.

pairs.left: She's been writing the book since she was in her twenties

exercises.prompt: Dr Fletcher ___ the same lecture to students for the last ten years.
exercises.explanation: A repeated activity over an extended period: the present perfect continuous fits best.
A figure states the result, so the plain present perfect is needed.

exercises.statement: He has been playing for the national team in 65 matches so far.
exercises.explanation: He has played for the national team in 65 matches so far. A specified number of occasions takes the present perfect.

exercises.prompt: Since 1950 influenza has claimed more than 50,000 lives in this country, and in 1957 alone around 6,000 people ___ in the outbreak.
exercises.explanation: In 1957 is a finished past time, so the past simple - not any perfect form - is right.

exercises.prompt: It's remarkable to think that since 1950 influenza ___ more than 50,000 lives in this country.
exercises.explanation: The number of lives is a result, so the present perfect continuous will not do.

exercises.prompt: Which form does each meaning call for?
categories: Present perfect - a result or a set number of occasions
Present perfect continuous - an extended or repeated activity

items.text: He's broken his finger and is in a lot of pain.
I've been playing squash and need a shower.
Miguel has been kicking a football against the wall all day.
He has played for the national team in 65 matches so far.
The workers have been calling for the chairman's resignation.
